In this video we're going to talk about a relatively new hot topic in DevOps and Cloud space, which is “platform engineering”. There is a lot of discussion going on, where some people are asking whether platform engineering replaces DevOps. Many people say it goes hand in hand and is rather an addition to DevOps, but in reality it's a bit more complicated than that. Platform engineering actually changes a lot of established rules we knew about DevOps, SRE and Cloud engineering, it changes the game and introduces some new rules.

So let's clearly define, what platform engineering exactly is, more interestingly, why was there even a need for this new role and how it evolved and of course how it compares to DevOps and Cloud engineering and does it really replace any of these roles?

HERE'S A FULL LIST OF DEVOPS ENGINEER INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
Q1. Tell me about yourself and why you want to work in this DevOps role?
Q2. What are the most important skills and qualities needed to work as a DevOps Engineer?

Q4. Tell me about the hardest day you’ve had as a DevOps Engineer?
Q5. What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Q7. Where do you see yourself in the future?
Q8. How do you handle stress and pressure at work?
Q9. What does DevOps mean to you and what is its purpose in our organization?
Q10. Tell me how DevOps differs from Agile / SDLC?
Q11. What is an inode on Linux?
Q12. In your opinion, which are the top DevOps tools and what are they used for?
Q13. Tell me how you'd go about optimizing a database?
Q14. What is garbage collection programming?
Q15. Talk me through the steps you would follow when checking physical memory on Linux?
Q16. Explain how you copy a local file to HDFS?
Q17. Describe how you would make a background process run?
Q18. Assuming there are no cookies, how would you make your application work?

videoTitle: Will AI replace DevOps Engineer? AI tools in DevOps 2024
videoDescription:
AI for DevOps | Will AI replace DevOps engineers | DevOps AI tools
In this DevOps video we will learning How AI and ML can be used in DevOps tasks like CICD, Monitoring, Logging, Deployments and more.
Along with Popular AI tools in devops and companies using AI with Devops.

Connect with me on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/nasiullha-chaudhari/ 

AI and DevOps are two fascinating fields in the tech world, and they're coming together in exciting ways. Many companies are exploring how AI can help improve their DevOps practices to make things smoother and more efficient.

With AI, we can automate repetitive tasks, optimize resource usage, and make better decisions.

A common question is whether AI will replace DevOps or the engineers working in this area. Well, AI can certainly enhance DevOps, but it won't replace the people. Instead, it will work alongside skilled DevOps engineers to make things even better.

AI Tools for DevOps:
1. Splunk
2. Harness
3. Amazon CodeGuru
4. PagerDuty
5. Dynatrace
6. Datadog
7. AppDynamics
8. Opsani
9. Puppet
10. Chef

These AI-powered tools, combined with popular DevOps platforms, enable organizations to accelerate their software development and delivery processes while ensuring greater reliability, scalability, and performance. The integration of AI in DevOps brings innovative solutions to complex challenges, allowing teams to focus on creating value for their customers.

1. Netflix: Netflix is well-known for its use of AI and machine learning to optimize content delivery, personalization, and infrastructure management in their DevOps workflows.
2. Google: Google has been a pioneer in AI research and has integrated AI tools and technologies into their DevOps processes to improve system performance and operational efficiency.
3. Facebook: Facebook uses AI and machine learning algorithms to optimize infrastructure, manage user data, and streamline their continuous deployment practices in DevOps.
4. Amazon: Amazon's AWS offers various AI-powered DevOps tools and services, such as Amazon CodeGuru, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeDeploy, to help developers automate tasks and improve software delivery.
5. Microsoft: Microsoft uses AI in their DevOps workflows to optimize Azure services, automate infrastructure management, and enhance developer productivity.
6. Spotify: Spotify uses AI-driven analytics and monitoring tools to gain insights into application performance and user behavior, enabling continuous improvements in their DevOps practices.
7. Twitter: Twitter employs AI and machine learning for infrastructure management, incident detection, and performance optimization in their DevOps pipelines.
8. Uber: Uber utilizes AI to manage large-scale infrastructure, improve data analysis
9. Airbnb: Airbnb leverages AI to optimize their continuous deployment and delivery pipelines
10. IBM: IBM has integrated AI technologies into their DevOps tools and solutions, such as IBM Cloud Pak for Applications, to facilitate intelligent automation and faster software delivery.

Adoption of AI in DevOps is not limited to these companies alone. More and more companies are embracing AI in their DevOps processes. By doing so, they can reduce manual work, spot issues faster, and deliver higher-quality software to their customers.

In conclusion, AI and DevOps make a fantastic team. They bring exciting possibilities for the future of software development, making it more efficient and effective. Embracing AI in DevOps can give your company a competitive edge in the tech world. So, let's welcome this exciting partnership!

videoTitle: DevOps Meetup Zurich 2024: Platform Engineering
videoDescription:
This video captures my presentation delivered at the DevOps Meetup in Zürich on January 25, 2024, where I delve into the prevalent challenges faced by traditional DevOps methodologies, characterized by isolated teams and fragmented value streams that impede efficiency. It explores DevOps as a holistic culture, mindset, and suite of technical practices designed to foster continuous value delivery, prioritize products over projects, and focus on customer-centric development. Additionally, I introduce Platform Engineering as a strategic evolution of DevOps aimed at mitigating the technical and operational complexities encountered when scaling DevOps in larger enterprises. Highlighting a collaborative project with LGT and Zühlke, I present the Platform Plane case study, demonstrating how an internal developer platform can streamline and standardize DevOps processes across various teams, thereby reducing cognitive load and enhancing productivity. This presentation goes beyond theoretical discussion, offering a hands-on demonstration of the Platform Plane and its functionalities, including Kubernetes as a service, API gateway, and Service Mesh, among others. It illustrates the vital role of Platform Engineering in enabling product teams to adopt DevOps more efficiently and effectively, leading to an optimized development lifecycle.

videoTitle: Guided DevOps Meditation
videoDescription:
Dive into a unique meditative experience designed specifically for the DevOps Engineer. In the hustle of ensuring seamless deployments and system operations, every DevOps professional deserves a moment to reboot, refresh, and recenter.

Whether you're in the midst of a complex project or wrapping up a day of successful deployments, this meditation will guide you to find serenity amidst the codes and systems.

🔗 Find tranquility amidst the binaries. Hit play and embark on a journey to the calm side of DevOps.

Don't forget to LIKE, SHARE, and SUBSCRIBE for more content dedicated to the DevOps community! 🚀👍

▬▬▬▬▬▬ S C R I P T  📜  ▬▬▬▬▬▬

"Begin by finding a serene place where you can sit undisturbed. As you prepare to delve into a state of calm, think of it as setting up the perfect environment for a seamless deployment."

"Sit or lie down in a comfortable position, ensuring that your back is straight and your hands rest lightly on your lap or by your sides. Close your eyes gently. Let's begin our system reboot."

"Start by taking a deep breath in, inhaling calmness and clarity, like the smooth initiation of a well-planned product. And exhale, releasing any system glitches or unwanted bugs from your mind."

"Imagine your mind as a server room. Each server represents a thought or a responsibility in your life. Some servers are humming busily, while others are quiet and in standby mode."

"Visualize a cooling system, a gust of fresh, clean air entering the room, stabilizing the temperature. This cooling breath ensures that every server, every thought, operates at its peak without overheating."

"As you continue breathing deeply, bring to mind a continuous integration and continuous deployment pipeline. With every inhale, new features and positive affirmations are integrated. With every exhale, new code is deployed to production."

"Imagine a monitoring dashboard, showcasing green status indicators. Your body is this system. Your heart rate, your breathing, your state of calm are all in optimal state - all systems operational and running smoothly."

"Think about the code commits. Sometimes, errors occur, and that's okay. Acknowledge them without judgment, fix them, and move on. For now, release any attachment to those errors, letting them float away like logs being archived."

"Your breathing is now your main server, your central command. Focus on its rhythm, the gentle in-and-out, the same predictable yet vital process, akin to the regular checks and balances in DevOps."

"Even in the face of challenges, remember that every system has its recovery procedure. Your mind, your spirit, and your body are no different. You have the resilience, the backup plans, and the capability for recovery."

"Slowly begin to transition, like smoothly moving from development to production. Become aware of your surroundings. Feel the chair or the floor supporting you, the gentle rhythm of your heart."

"When you're ready, with the confidence of a successful code deployment, open your eyes. As you go back into the world, remember that just like in DevOps, balance, continuous improvement, and adaptation are key."

videoTitle: 😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
videoDescription:
😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
Really? No 😉.
Don't panic and check out the talk 🎞 I had with Pia Wiedermayer on this topic.

Is DevOps really the reason why testing and quality assurance (QA) employees are being increasingly automated out of a job?
Pia Wiedermayer, Head of QA, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, discuss different ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testing and QA specialists into the agile team culture.

Insight: 
- DevOps is often equated with automation
- What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities?
- Testers offer a wealth of experience that can be incorporated into the
agile team culture

Software testing and quality assurance are changing. Topics such as agility, DevOps and automation strongly influence existing roles and areas of responsibility in software quality assurance as well as during the entire software life cycle. Standard testing and QA roles no longer exist in many (project) organisations. Dedicated testing teams are increasingly a thing of the past.

What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities? Is there no room for them anymore? Are their skills and expertise no longer needed?

DevOps is often equated with automation. Is DevOps responsible for automating employees out of a job? What is behind the hype and who or what is DevOps actually?

Pia Wiedermayer, Head of Quality Assurance https://www.linkedin.com/in/piawiedermayer/, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, at Zühlke Switzerland tackle these questions. They talk about the challenges in their projects, examine roles and tasks and reveal new paths for professional and personal development. They also discuss ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testers into the agile team culture and whether automation is the new testing.

videoTitle: Introduction of DevOps Certified Professional Program

The program also emphasizes the cultural aspects of DevOps, focusing on collaboration, communication, and fostering a culture of continuous improvement.

Upon completing the program, participants have the opportunity to earn a DevOps Certified Professional certification, which validates their proficiency and expertise in DevOps principles and practices. This certification can enhance career prospects and demonstrate a commitment to professional development in the field of DevOps.

The DevOps Certified Professional Program is suitable for professionals from various backgrounds, including software development, system administration, operations, quality assurance, and project management. It is particularly beneficial for individuals seeking to transition into DevOps roles or enhance their existing DevOps skills.

Overall, the DevOps Certified Professional Program provides a comprehensive and structured learning path for individuals looking to build a strong foundation in DevOps practices and technologies. 📎 Attachments: Any files or attachments related to the issue or work item should be synced to ensure easy access and collaboration.

📌 Work Item Type/Issue Type: The type of work item or issue, such as bug, feature, or task. Syncing this field provides clarity and consistency in categorizing different types of work.

In this episode, Microsoft Technical Trainer Andrew Conniff introduces Module 01: Introduction to DevOps. You’ll explore DevOps as the union of people, process, and products to enable continuous delivery of value, and learn why continuous improvement and cycle-time optimization are essential in modern software delivery.

You’ll also examine key DevOps practices, including CI/CD, monitoring and logging, cloud fundamentals, infrastructure as code, microservices, and containers. videoTitle: BTAIH E03 · Mohamed Daoudi, DevOps Engineer · Can AI Replace DevOps Engineers?
videoDescription:
My third guest on BTAIH is Mohamed Daoudi, a DevOps engineer whose path took him from ENSA and self-taught Linux and Docker to early-stage companies, large-scale cloud systems at Oracle, and independent consulting.

We get into what happens when AI stops being a chatbot and starts touching real infrastructure: writing scripts, handling repetitive migrations, executing commands, configuring CI/CD, connecting hosting and domains, and helping ship a working website in less than 24 hours.

It is a practical conversation, not a hype one. Where AI genuinely makes a DevOps engineer faster, where it turns 100 lines into 10,000, and why giving an agent access to your systems is only useful when you still understand the infrastructure underneath it.

About Mohamed

Mohamed Daoudi is a DevOps engineer with experience across startups, service companies, Oracle Cloud and independent consulting. His work has included CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, incident management and keeping production systems stable at scale.

Through this tutorial, you will learn how to set up and configure ECS services for your applications.

🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

videoDescription:
DevOps とは？
～エンジニアじゃなくてもわかる ITトレンド解説 ～

はい、マジセミ寺田です！皆さんこんにちは！今日は DevOps について解説をしていきます。
エンジニアじゃなくてもわかるように簡単に解説していきますのでよろしくお願いします！
私はマジセミという、IT関連のWebセミナーを年600回程度運営しています。
他のテーマの動画もたくさんUPしてますので是非そちらもご覧ください！
今日のテーマは DevOps ですね、DevOps ってなに？って思われるかもしれないんですけども"Dev"と"Ops"をくっつけた造語なんです。
"Dev"っていうのは"デブロップメント"システムの開発です。"Ops"は"オペレーション"、システムの運用です。
昔は開発と運用が分かれていて、組織も分かれていて、場合によっては会社も分かれてるケースもよくありました。
なんで分かれていたか？というと性格が違うからなんです。
開発はどんどん良いものを作っていきたいと考えているのですが、新しい機能を動かす時や何らかのイベントがある時はトラブルが起きやすいんですね。
逆にいうと何にも変更がないまま運用している分にはそんなにトラブルは起きません。
なので新しい機能を入れるとか改善するとかそういう事をやりたくないというのが運用チームの立場でなんです。
こういった、今までの組織の在り方を理解した上で、現代ではDX（デジタルトランスフォーメーション）が非常に注目されていますが、その中で重要なのはスピードです。
今まではシステムを開発して機能の改善をして、それが使えるようになるのは１年後だとか短くても３ヶ月後という感覚でした。
しかしその感覚だと追いつかなくなってしまいます。
来週、もっと早ければ明日にでも使って欲しい、とスピードが求められています。
そんな中、今までのように開発のチームと運用のチームが分かれていると、全然スピードが追いつかないという事で、もうその工程を１つにしてしまって、開発したらすぐに運用出来るようにする、といった具合に、そもそもの組織のあり方を含めて根本的に作業の進め方を変えていくというのが" DevOps "の考え方や方法論です。
また、今回のセミナー（https://majisemi.com/e/c/dynatrace-20210305）では2021年の米国の最新動向についても紹介しています。
これは" DevOps "だけじゃなくて他にも"AIOps"や”コンテナ”などの最新動向についても解説していますので、" DevOps "や米国のIT最新動向に関心のある方は見ていただければと思います！

videoTitle: DKT 96 | Mock-интервью DevOps: AWS EKS, Terraform, Kubernetes, AI + много практики
videoDescription:
Mock-интервью с Николаем Лебедевым - DevOps/SRE-инженер, 17 лет в Linux, 4 года AWS EKS. Stack: Terraform, Flux, Cassandra, Kafka, Vault, SOPS. Два часа - много практики, много каверзных вопросов.

ЧТО СПРАШИВАЛИ

☁️ AWS: EKS и IRSA, VPC с нуля (CIDR, multi-AZ, multi-region), managed K8s vs self-hosted, Elasticache, Golden Signals и метрики SRE.

🔧 TERRAFORM: state как главный ресурс и blast radius, drift detection, locking, антипаттерны, когда нужен модуль vs ресурс.

🐳 KUBERNETES: полный путь kubectl apply (admission → etcd → scheduler → kubelet), OOMKill vs eviction (кто посылает SIGKILL), QoS-классы, RBAC subresources (pods/log, pods/exec), Deployment vs DaemonSet vs StatefulSet.

🤖 AI ДЛЯ DEVOPS: токенизатор и как текст становится вектором, RAG под капотом (chunking, vector DB, similarity), RAG vs fine-tuning, безопасность heap dump в LLM, prompt injection vs jailbreak.

💻 LIVE TASKS: разбор сломанного Flask + Redis (nobody user, env vars), Contains Duplicate на Python, GitOps pipeline в GitHub Actions (SHORT_SHA, cross-repo commit).

ГОСТЬ

Николай Лебедев, Cloud SRE Engineer. 17 лет в Linux-инфраструктуре, 4 года продуктовой работы с AWS EKS и GitOps (Flux + Bitbucket, миграция в GitHub Actions).

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

Production just went down with a 502 Bad Gateway after a critical deployment. Jenkins pipeline triggered it, the deployment failed — and users were impacted.

Checked logs — the app was failing health checks

Root cause: a missing production environment variable

Rolled back the deployment safely using Helm

Fixed the configuration and stopped further rollouts

Patched the CI/CD pipeline to catch such issues early

videoTitle: Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeeper
videoDescription:
Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeepers 

Timestamps:

Theory/Concepts : 00:00
Hands on/Practical : 09:00

github repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/opa-gatekeeper.git

Concepts :

OPA Gatekeeper: Policy and Governance for Kubernetes

What is OPA:

The Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack. OPA provides a high-level declarative language that lets us specify policies as code and simple APIs to offload policy decision-making from our software. We can use OPA to enforce policies in microservices, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more. 
In kubernetes, OPA uses admission controllers.

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a specialized project providing first-class integration between OPA and Kubernetes.
OPA Gatekeeper adds the following on top of plain OPA:
● An extensible, parameterized policy library.
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for instantiating the policy library (aka “constraints”).
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for extending the policy library (aka “constraint templates”).
● Audit functionality.

Why you need Gatekeeper?

As a Platform DevOps engineer managing multiple Kubernetes clusters for various projects, you face challenges when users deploy applications without adhering to best practices. Key issues include:
  1.     Lack of ownership unless users apply labels themselves.
  2.     No resource limits, leading to high costs.
  3.     Untrusted images impacting other applications.
  4.     Security and best practice violations across clusters.

To address these, we need governance to enforce limits and rules via policies. OPA Gatekeeper can be configured to implement these policies, ensuring best practices are followed.

videoTitle: Neurodiversity and the Essence of DevOps - Jeff Sussna
videoDescription:
It’s been gratifying to see the DevOps community take up the challenge of making empathy the essence of what we do. We should be proud of ourselves as an example to other organizational transformation approaches. We still, though, have room to grow. Whether it’s NoOps, or cloud-native chauvinism, or labeling people on the autism spectrum as lacking the capacity for empathy, we create subtle separations and exclusions through language and practice.

I would like to use my experience as a person with autism to reflect on the true meaning of empathy as the essence of DevOps. People on the spectrum are typically viewed as lacking something. In the process, our strengths and value get ignored. Real empathy means looking for wisdom and capability across differences. How do we do that in a comprehensive way? What are the obstacles to doing so in our current approaches to DevOps? How can overcoming those obstacles provide a model for digital transformation, and for healthy organizations, that transcends dev and ops?

RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker — it acts as a middleman between different parts of a system that need to communicate asynchronously.
It uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) as its core protocol.

In simpler terms:

It receives messages from producers (applications sending data),

Stores them temporarily in queues,

And delivers them to consumers (applications receiving data).

This helps decouple systems — the sender and receiver don’t need to be active at the same time.

⚙️ 2. Why Use RabbitMQ?

✅ Decoupling – Producers don’t need to know who consumes messages.
✅ Asynchronous communication – Improves system responsiveness.
✅ Load balancing – Messages can be distributed across multiple consumers.
✅ Reliability – Ensures message delivery even if parts of the system fail.
✅ Scalability – You can add more queues or consumers easily.
✅ Flexible routing – Decide how messages flow using exchanges and routing keys.

🔩 3. Core RabbitMQ Concepts
🏭 Producers

Applications that send messages to RabbitMQ.
They don’t send messages directly to a queue but to an exchange.

🎯 Exchanges

An exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules.

Exchange types:

Type Behavior Example Use Case
Direct Routes messages to queues whose binding key exactly matches routing key Task queues
Fanout Broadcasts all messages to all queues bound to it Notifications, pub/sub
Topic Routes messages based on pattern matching (* and #) Selective subscriptions
Headers Routes based on header attributes Advanced filtering

videoTitle: Salesforce Devops -- What Is Next? Dreamforce 2021
videoDescription:
DF 21 Inspiring Excellence 

Slides PDF with notes 
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1a-bsFs1rY3ofUJrusbcW80Q7bcSym6Oy/view?usp=sharing

Slide 1
Welcome everyone to Dreamforce 21 Inspiring Excellence sessions. I’m Vernon Keenan from SalesforceDevops.net in Oakland, California. Let’s commit!
Slide 2
I’ve spent 2021 curating and cataloging the companies, products and services that help Salesforce customers deliver enterprise applications. Here is what I learned.
Slide 3
Let’s get our arms around DEVOPS. It seems to be the latest Salesforce buzzword. And it has turned into a powerful word indeed. 
If you are “doing devops” today that indicates you are managing how to build the means of production for your organization. If you want to exist as an enterprise in the digital domain, then you need devops to have the automation capabilities that delivers enterprise app updates and continuously improves app value.
The origin of the devops concept started in 2007 when its main push was to find ways to obliterate barriers between app developers and system operators. Developers became frustrated with the time it took to iterate on software builds when dealing with operations teams. 
This diagram from Azure DevOps website portrays it beautifully. It shows how better communication results in the collaboration and teamwork necessary to manage, develop, deliver and operate a live application. It shows the main benefit of using devops, which is to have a mechanism that allows teams to respond quickly to user behavior.
Another key to the success of DevOps is the idea of metrics and observability, and how that dovetails with agile management philosophies, such as tying metrics into objectives and key results. In fact, I’d say that Devops and Agile have been kissing behind the barn, and a new unified app production perspective is evolving which I call Devops 3.0.
Slide 4
One reason why devops has gained prominence is because it represents the convergence of three huge business forces. First, Salesforce is now a business transformation platform, and not just a CRM. Since the platform is strategic for many more businesses, executives need a governance harness and better visibility into app production activities.
Next, an all-pervasive force in modern information technology is the incredibly rich and diverse world of cloud native computing. When engineers at Uber, Salesforce, Netflix, or a new startup need tools to build an online service from scratch, they are using cloud native computing tools and services.
Until 2017, Salesforce was largely a closed platform to the cloud native world. Then SFDX-CLI was introduced and that really made Salesforce devops take off. It allowed LINUX scripts and cloud native tools to now interact with configuration information in Salesforce. That subsequently lets cloud native automation tools like Jenkins and Azure Devops act as a command server in a release management pipeline orchestration scheme. 
Slide 5
I made this relationship classification system to help figure out if all the boxes are checked when you are building an continuous app delivery system. This diagram gives you an idea of the complexity involved in a Salesforce devops solution. So, the good news is that we have good roadmaps for how to build a devops solution, but the bad news is that there are a lot of things to do and a lot of systems that need to be tied together.
That’s where a key software vendor like GEARSET comes into play. Salesforce devops platform vendors are all working to check these boxes off for you, so they are worth a look if you are getting started.
Slide 6
Now, let’s take that mess of products and reorganize them into this stack. This summary shows how Salesforce devops is first controlled by the governance functions, which collects metrics and data from the app production teams. Next, these teams of architects, developers, admins, business analysts, and constituents use a consistent set of automation and deployment tools to continuously optimize apps.
One key thing that makes this different for Salesforce app is the curious way in which we must manage metadata. A key function in Salesforce devops is that metadata must be ingested, analyzed, queried, and dynamically updated. When updating a live org, this is the only way for an app production team to work together. There must be intelligent metadata management in any Salesforce devops platform in order to optimize your release management processes. 
Slide 7
Now we are expanding the pyramid to show some of the functional layers in a full-fledged Salesforce devops solution, pretty much like what you get with Gearset. Here we can see some of the more familiar names and details that go into creating a full devops solution.

Slide 8
Now, let’s explode this out some more. Ben McCarthy of SalesforceBen and I worked together to design this Period Table of Devops Solutions,

videoTitle: What is Secure DevOps?
videoDescription:
It’s surprisingly easy for hackers to impersonate authorized users of your corporate Git environment. Why? Because your developers can access it using their personal accounts, which are not tied to a corporate identity. That makes it difficult for IT to control access. And because contributors can sign the author field of a commit with anything they like, IT can’t track who is really authoring these commits.

Just as bad, contributors are committing code on unauthorized machines, often without even logging into the Git web service, evading all access controls.

This leaves your software components vulnerable to unauthorized access and tampering, which can lead to malicious code getting distributed to all of your clients.

With Secure DevOps by Beyond Identity, you can ensure that only your developers check in code to your repo. And that all commits came from an authorized user and device. All without impacting software velocity.

videoTitle: What's the goal of Platform Engineering? #shorts #devops #platformengineering
videoDescription:
Watch the full video: https://youtu.be/JAblex0uS4k

What’s the goal of Platform Engineering? Platform Engineering focusses on the building the infrastructure and the systems that are needed for running your applications and supporting your application throughout the software life cycle. So,  the goal  is to support the developers in the organisation and treat them as customers. That’s why we have in platform engineering the concept of IDP Internal developer platform.
 
So, this platform is treated as an actual product and the customers of the product are the developers.
What is the role of the IDP?
It is to create a thin layer on top of the toolchain that is used inside the organisation to standardise the processes and help developers to have one way to deploy into production

videoTitle: Git Plumbing vs Porcelain #Git #GitHub #GitLab #BitBucket #DevOps #GitOps #Python #Java #JavaScript
videoDescription:
Have you heart the terms Git plumbing and Git Porcelain?

Ever wondered what the different between Git porcelain vs plumbing was?

For the most part, the porcelain is the most commonly used Git files such as:

- git init
- git add
- git commit
- git revert
- git merge
- git rebase
- git reset

That's the Git porcelain, and you won't get your hands too dirty when you touch it.

The Git plumbing? That's typically the config stuff in the hidden .git folder, including things like:

- Refspec
-Packfiles
- The HEAD Pointer
- Git References
- Remote References
- Transfer Protocols
- Garbage Collector
- Recovery files
- Tree Objects
- Environment variables

Hopefully you don't have to get your hands dirty with the Git plumbing too often. It's nice to stick with the Git porcelain.

But at the same time, plumbers do make a lot of money!

videoTitle: devopsdaysNYC 2020 - Day 2 - Thomas Limoncelli - Low-Context DevOps
videoDescription:
Low-Context DevOps: Helping DevOps find answers faster

Problem: Knowledge frustration is when siloed knowledge blocks you from doing your job. Yes, you can escalate or bother another coworker, but wouldn’t it be better if you had the instructions you needed when you needed it? Knowledge frustration is common for new people getting up to speed, experienced people moving between projects, and oncall engineers that receive an alert they’ve never seen before.

Solution: In this talk, I’ll show how to use the anthropology concept of high-context/low-context societies to eliminate knowledge frustration on DevOps/SRE teams. The result is improved productivity, continuous improvement, and a more enjoyable work environment.

Edward T. Hall was an American anthropologist who coined the phrase “high-context culture,” a culture where there are many unspoken rules. One must know a large amount of context to survive. Low-context cultures have the rules explicitly stated. This model describes engineering teams as well.

This is a talk about how to create a low-context culture where documentation is created incrementally, maintained continuously, and available just in time. Eliminate the “I’ll document it later” syndrome.

videoTitle: Liquibase Tutorial 2026 | Master Database Version Control for DevOps Jobs
videoDescription:
What is Liquibase, and why is database version control becoming an important skill for modern software development and DevOps careers?

In this Liquibase tutorial for beginners, we explain how Liquibase works as a database change management and deployment tool used by developers, DBAs, DevOps engineers, and software teams to manage database changes safely across Development, QA, UAT, and Production environments.

Liquibase works like Git for databases. Just as Git tracks application code changes, Liquibase tracks database schema changes using changelogs and changesets. Instead of manually running SQL scripts across multiple servers, teams can define database changes as code and automate database deployments through CI/CD pipelines.

You’ll understand the fundamentals of Liquibase, database version control, database migration, schema management, changelogs, changesets, CI/CD automation, DevOps, and database deployment.

If you are preparing for a career as a DevOps Engineer, Software Developer, Database Administrator (DBA), Cloud Engineer, or Release Engineer, learning database automation and version control can help you build practical, job-ready skills.

Learn modern DevOps and database deployment skills that are relevant to today’s technology careers and the evolving software industry.

In this video, you will learn:
• What Liquibase is and why organizations use it
• How Liquibase changesets and changelogs work

videoTitle: 5 DevOps Interview Questions (2023)
videoDescription:
Follow me on LinkedIn at: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jarrettcoggin/

----
In this video, I wanted to go over some DevOps Interview Questions that I've asked candidates for DevOps Engineering positions, both for roles as fellow coworkers and for roles which would report to me. I provide tips for devops interview questions and help you understand why an interviewer might ask some of these questions. These are just some of the devops questions you'll get in an interview.

What does DevOps mean to you?

What is a CI/CD pipeline and why is it important for a team to implement? What do you need to implement a CI/CD pipeline? What would you focus on first? How would you improve a team's existing CI/CD pipeline?

Outside of CI/CD pipelines, what other responsibilities fall onto DevOps Engineers?

What is [INSERT TOOL HERE]? What is it used for? Do you have experience using [TOOL]? If you have used it, what did you like about it? What did you not like about it? What are the alternatives? (This line of questioning lends well to cost-benefit analysis, including build-vs.-buy decisions, which are especially important for small companies with few people that need to execute quickly.)

What types of release processes have you been part of in the past? How have you improved those processes?

videoTitle: Every DevOps Tool Explained (And the Only 10 You Need in 2026)
videoDescription:
There are over 1,000 tools in the CNCF landscape, and every single one claims to be essential for DevOps. Most of them are not. The ones that are fall into about 10 categories that have barely changed in a decade.

In this video I walk you through the entire DevOps toolchain: every category, the tools that actually matter inside each one, and what each one is genuinely good for. From Git and CI/CD to containers, Kubernetes, Terraform and OpenTofu, GitOps with Argo CD, observability, security, platform engineering, and the new AI layer (MCP, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent).

The biggest mistake I see junior engineers make is learning tools instead of learning the category the tool sits in. Tools get replaced. Categories don't.

1:06 Prerequisites: Linux and networking
1:17 Version control (Git, GitHub, GitLab)

13:42 The stack I'd learn if I started today

Git, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana, Trivy and Vault, Backstage. One per category, learned deep. Swapping any of them out later takes a weekend, not a career.

videoTitle: How Apps Update Without Downtime (Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary)
videoDescription:
How do apps update without downtime, meaning without ever going offline? This video follows one bank app to show how it gets a new version while people keep using it.

Behind your bank app, the bank runs many copies of the same program. A load balancer sends each tap you make to a copy that is ready.

What you will learn:
- The 3 steps of a rolling update: the load balancer, swapping a few copies at a time, and the health check
- Why the app stays online while old copies shut down
- How a team can roll back (go back to the old version) if the new version has a bug
- Blue-green deployment: two full server sets and one quick switch
- Canary release: how a small group gets the new version first, and why it is named after the birds that coal miners once used to warn of danger

If a friend gets a new feature before you, it may be a canary test.

videoTitle: Linux Commands for DevOps and SRE: grep, awk, sed, find and More
videoDescription:
10 Linux commands every DevOps engineer and SRE should know: grep, awk, sed, find, head, tail, sort, uniq, wc and cut. For each one, you get the 2 to 3 options you will actually use on the job, with real examples on nginx logs and system files.

Master these and you can answer questions about your system in seconds, not minutes.


COMMANDS FROM THIS SESSION

1. grep
Search for a string (add -i to ignore case):
grep "error" error.log
Search recursively through a directory:
grep -r "error" /var/log
Match 4xx and 5xx status codes with extended regex:
grep -E "4[0-9]{2}|5[0-9]{2}" access.log

2. awk
Print columns 1 and 6, with ":" as the separator:
awk -F: '{print $1 "   " $6}' /etc/passwd
Print lines where column 1 matches a value:
awk '$1 == "127.0.0.1"' access.log
Search for text and print specific columns:
awk '/error/ {print $17 $18}' error.log

3. sed
Replace every occurrence and print the result:
sed 's/10.0.2.200/10.0.2.120/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/backend.conf
Replace inside the file itself:
sed -i 's/10.0.2.200/10.0.2.120/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/backend.conf
Replace every IP address using extended regex:
sed -i -E 's/[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}/127.0.0.1/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/newbackend.conf

4. find
Find files by name:
find . -name "*.log"
Find files modified in the last 2 days:
find /var/log -type f -mtime -2
Run a command on every match:
find . -name "*.log" -exec gzip {} \;

5. head
First 10 lines:
head access.log
First 30 lines:
head -n 30 access.log

6. tail
Last 10 lines:
tail access.log
Last 30 lines:
tail -n 30 access.log
Follow the file live:
tail -f access.log

7. sort
Alphabetical sort:
ls | sort
Numeric sort, smallest directory first:
du -hk -d 1 | sort -n
Sort file systems by usage, highest first:
df -kh | sort -rk5

8. uniq
Unique client IPs sending bad requests:
grep " 400 " /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq
The same, with a count for each IP:
grep " 400 " /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c

9. wc
Count lines:
wc -l access.log
Count lines, words and characters:
wc access.log

10. cut
Extract fields 1 and 2:
cut -d: -f1,2 /etc/passwd
Extract fields 1 to 3:
cut -d: -f1-3 /etc/passwd

TWO ONE-LINERS FROM THIS SESSION

Top 10 client IPs hitting your server:
awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10

Largest log files on your system:
sudo find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" -exec du -k {} \; | sort -rn | head -n 5

videoTitle: Stop False Test Failures: Test Data Stage in Azure DevOps Pipeline

videoTitle: Your CI Pipeline Didn't Change. It Still Leaked Secrets.
videoDescription:
#devsecops  #cicd  #supplychainsecurity 
On September 16, pipelines nobody had touched started stealing secrets again, and not one line in their workflow files had changed.

This is a calm, CVE-by-CVE breakdown of the DevOps toolchain flaws that were exploited, or newly flagged as exploited, in the 30 days before October 5, 2026. We cover the re-enabled compromised GitHub Actions carrying the Mini Shai-Hulud payload, the JFrog Artifactory empty-string authentication bypass (CVE-2026-82329, CVSS 9.8), the Kestra suffix-check bypass (CVE-2026-49869, CVSS 10, added to CISA KEV on September 2), and the TeamCity agent-protocol deserialization flaw (CVE-2026-63077) now linked to ransomware. We then work through the backlog: the September 2 Jenkins advisory, kubectl cp path traversal on Windows (CVE-2026-19444) and containerd hardening. For each one you get how it was found, how attackers exploit it, and the exact order to follow: detect, patch, rotate, revoke, verify. The video ends with a triage list your team can start on Monday morning.

videoTitle: Kubernetes Secret Missing From One Pod: Why the Cluster Looked Fine
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

Two pods, one Deployment, one image, and one of them was missing a Secret key that already existed. The cluster said everything was fine.

THE NEWS. A platform engineer, Ahmed Tariq, found the mismatch during a post-deploy check, before any user noticed (Cloud Native Now, October 6, 2026). The Secret held the new key, both pod specs referenced it, and one Deployment owned both. Only asking each running process settled it, with a loop that compares variable NAMES, never values. One pod printed present, and the other printed missing.

THE SETUP. The values lived in Azure Key Vault. The Secrets Store CSI Driver mounted them through a SecretProviderClass and mirrored them into a normal Kubernetes Secret, which the app read as environment variables through envFrom.

TWIST 1, TWO CLOCKS. The driver syncs the Secret only when a pod mounts it. Environment variables are written once, when the container starts, and a running process never sees a later Secret update. Only a restart re-reads them.

TWIST 2, HELM'S ORDER. Helm 4.2.3 sorts a release by kind, not by file name. Deployment is kind 29 of the 38 kinds on its built-in install list; SecretProviderClass is a custom kind, and in the Helm source an unknown kind is last. We ran Helm 4.2.3's own sorter on two templates named so that a file-name sort would put the provider class first, and it installed the Deployment first. So one new pod mounted the old provider class before the new one arrived. The author kept no pod timestamps, mount events or CSI logs, so he calls that exact sequence an inference.

THE SECOND APP. A second app, deployed with plain kubectl apply, applied the provider class after the rollout and the health check. All 3 of its running pods missed the new key until a restart.

THE FIXES. First, the order: apply the provider class before the rollout, so new pods mount the current version. Second, a gate after every rollout that reads the expected key names from the SecretProviderClass, checks every running pod, never prints a secret value, restarts the Deployment once on a miss, and fails the deploy on a second miss. The gate drawn on screen is written out for this Short and was executed against a mock cluster in four cases (all present, fixed by the restart, still missing, unreadable pod).

TWIST 3, THE GATE'S OWN HOLE. The shipped gate logged a warning and SKIPPED any pod it could not read, so an unreadable pod passed. The safer version counts a failed inspection as a failure. One detail we tested: the article's fail-closed snippet flags the pod only when the script runs with set -o pipefail, because the exit status of the last command in the pipe hides the failed exec otherwise.

THE HEALTH CHECK. The health endpoint kept returning 200 OK the whole time, because it never touched the feature that used the new key, so Kubernetes had no reason to replace the pod.

THE LESSON. A Secret shows what Kubernetes stored. Only the process shows what it read. Apply the class first. Roll the pods. Check every process.

videoTitle: Qué es DevOps: cultura, automatización y entrega continua | C04
videoDescription:
Qué es DevOps: cultura, automatización y entrega continua | C04

¿Cómo llevar una mejora del software hasta sus usuarios y operarla con seguridad? DevOps conecta personas, procesos y tecnología durante todo el ciclo de vida. En este capítulo distinguimos integración continua, entrega continua y despliegue continuo, y recorremos calidad, seguridad, observación y recuperación.

Seguimos una mejora de nuestra app móvil ficticia de actividades personales. Diferenciamos cambios del servidor, actualizaciones de la app, liberación de funciones y adopción de versiones, con las condiciones reales de App Store y Google Play.

La aplicación, sus cifras y las decisiones son ficticias. Retención D30 de 30 % a 40 % y primera actividad dentro de 24 horas de 45 % a 65 % son metas trimestrales, no resultados conseguidos ni referencias del sector. D30 exige crear una actividad relevante en el día calendario 30 y completar la observación de las cohortes elegibles.

Este capítulo combina mi experiencia laboral y profesional en desarrollo de software, trabajo con equipos ágiles y prácticas DevOps con las referencias oficiales que encontrarás a continuación. Comparto una perspectiva práctica para conectar estos conceptos con los retos del trabajo cotidiano.
